title: Bennett Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Bennett wells have a 360-foot median depth and typically cost $24,000-$37,200 finished, based on local permit and cost data.
h1: Bennett, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Bennett sits over the Denver Basin, where well conditions can change across the plains even between nearby properties. Records within five miles show a 360-foot median well depth, with half of reported wells between 90 and 480 feet.

That is useful for estimating a project, but it is not a guarantee for a particular lot. Before buying, compare nearby permits, confirm the intended use, and have a Colorado well professional review the site, access, septic layout, and likely drilling conditions.

sections.heading: Bennett well depth: plan for the Denver Basin
sections.html:
Most Bennett-area wells are completed in the 300-to-600-foot range: that depth mix accounts for 54% of records. Another 25% are under 100 feet, while 11% fall between 100 and 300 feet and 10% are 600 feet or deeper.

The local range is wide. The middle half runs from 90 to 480 feet, the 90th-percentile depth is 592 feet, and the deepest record reaches 2,821 feet. For a driller's bid, use the 360-foot median as a starting point, not a promised completion depth. Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the selected aquifer, and the individual lot can all change the final depth.

sections.heading: How much water do Bennett wells produce?
sections.html:
Among Bennett-area permits that report a pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is tightly grouped between 10.0 and 14.0 gallons per minute. About 76% report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 23% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute in this dataset. That is encouraging for ordinary household planning, but a permit yield is not the same as guaranteed long-term production. Ask for the well completion report, pumping information, storage capacity, and the permit's allowed use before relying on a number.

sections.heading: Bennett water levels and the recent trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median of 158 feet below ground, with the middle half between 90 and 245 feet. A buyer should account for that water level when reviewing pump setting, electrical requirements, and the cost of lifting water to the house.

The decade figures show a deeper reported water level in newer measurements: the median was 130 feet below surface in the 2010s and 180 feet in the 2020s. That difference suggests the measured water level may be lower in the more recent records, but it does not by itself prove a basin-wide decline. Measurements may come from different wells, aquifers, seasons, and testing conditions.

sections.heading: Bennett drilling history and local permit records
sections.html:
Bennett has a long drilling record. Permits were issued from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The busiest decades in the records were the 1990s, with 353 permits, and the 2000s, with 401. There are 1,758 wells in the Colorado DWR permit records, including 919 recorded as constructed.

The most common drillers in this record are Crandall Drilling & Pump Service, including Crandall Jr. and Howard H., with 357 records; Don Eastwood Drilling Inc., with 138; and Crandall Drlg. & Trenching Inc, with 89. These names help when tracking down older completion details, but the current contractor still needs to evaluate the lot.

sections.heading: What a new Bennett well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $50-$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 360-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $18,000-$25,200.

A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $24,000-$37,200. Treat that as a planning range rather than a fixed quote. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, a longer trench, or an unexpected completion can move the price. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the well reaches a dry or inadequate zone.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying near Bennett
sections.html:
The permit records identify Denver Basin aquifer wells throughout this area, with permits also naming the Denver and Upper Arapahoe aquifers. The records include 692 wells in an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, 376 in the Denver aquifer, and 199 in the Upper Arapahoe aquifer. Fractured zones can be less predictable than their nearby neighbors, so location-specific records matter.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. Within about ten miles are 93 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 27 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are no historic mine features mapped in that search, but that does not replace testing. Test existing water for appropriate contaminants, verify septic setbacks and soil suitability, and confirm that the well location leaves room for the house, septic system, driveway, and future repairs.

sections.heading: A practical lot check for Bennett buyers
sections.html:
Start with the closest completed wells, not just the countywide median. Compare their depths, reported yields, static levels, aquifers, uses, and construction dates. A household well is commonly permitted for exempt domestic use, but the permit controls what the well may legally serve. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses or changes.

For a buildable lot, confirm legal access for a large drilling rig, a staging area, power routing, and separation from septic components. Budget from the local finished-well range, then keep room for sitework and treatment. The nearby records for Strasburg, Watkins, Brick Center, Comanche Creek, Byers, and Aetna Estates can provide useful context, but the Bennett lot's own neighboring wells are the better comparison.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Bennett, Colorado?
faq.a: Bennett wells in the five-mile permit area have a median reported depth of 360 feet. The middle half runs from 90 to 480 feet, while 54% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record is 2,821 feet. Those figures are useful for budgeting, but the depth on a specific lot can vary with aquifer and geology.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Bennett?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 360-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $18,000-$25,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $24,000-$37,200. A written bid should explain how pricing changes if the hole must be deeper or produces inadequate water.

faq.q: How much water does a Bennett well produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 11.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 14.0. About 76% of reported wells produce 5-15 gallons per minute and 23% report more than 15. These are permit-record figures, not a promise for an un drilled well or a guarantee of long-term supply.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Bennett, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The area has 93 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 27 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. Have the existing well tested by a qualified laboratory, review nearby environmental information, and test a new well after construction before using it for drinking.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Bennett?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 130 feet below surface in the 2010s and 180 feet in the 2020s. That shows deeper measurements in the newer decade and may indicate lower water levels, but the data come from different wells and conditions. It is not enough by itself to prove a basin-wide decline or predict one property's future level.
